item.title: You Won’t Know It Was the Last Time
item.description:
Mindfulness

You Won’t Know It Was the Last Time

Personal Perspective: You are living moments now that you will one day miss.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Most of life’s meaningful endings happen quietly, so we often recognize them only afterward.
  • Familiarity makes recurring experiences feel unlimited, causing us to overlook their value.
  • Research suggests that perceiving an ending as near can increase engagement and well-being.
  • Pausing to notice sensory details can help us be present before an ordinary moment becomes a memory.

We have 3 kids, and our little one is six. Yesterday I saw him playing with LEGO pieces by himself while narrating the game out loud — voicing the different characters. He was so absorbed in the game; it was joyful to watch. My other two children are older — they have left this way of playing behind, and I suddenly realized something: this might have been the last time I saw one of my children play in this way.

When something ends with a formal ceremony, we clearly recognize the ending. High school graduation is a good example, which formally marks the end of childhood and the beginning of a new stage in life. The same applies to retirement ceremonies and funerals; they formally acknowledge that something significant has ended.

holding hands
Source: Gerlat / Pixabay

But most of life’s endings arrive unannounced. Silent.

How was I supposed to know last month that it was the last time my child asked me to carry him in my arms? This is a bittersweet ending – my kids are growing up, which is beautiful. But at the same time, many things that I loved are ending. And I need to let go, whether I want it or not.

Some of these endings for you might include:

  • The last time your child reaches for your hand while crossing the road.
  • The last bedtime story.
  • The last spontaneous visit from a certain friend.
  • The last time your entire family sits around the same table.
  • The last time your body can do something effortlessly.
  • The last conversation before a relationship slowly fades.

As they happen, these moments rarely feel significant. Only later do we realize how special they were. It’s natural; the mind quickly turns repeated experiences into background scenery. Familiarity creates an assumption of continuation: If something happened yesterday and today, we expect it to happen tomorrow.

We neglect ordinary moments because we believe they are unlimited.

Think of Jaime Kurtz’s (2008) study on perceived temporal scarcity. She took two groups of college students and encouraged them to think of their graduation as being close or far into the future. Those who thought their graduation was coming up soon were more engaged in their college experiences and reported higher levels of well-being.

article continues after advertisement

In other words, being aware that the ending might be coming soon can help us appreciate the experience and participate more fully.

And so, when I notice my child playing or asking to hold my hand, I pause and internally embrace the moment. Realizing that the end might be near makes me more present and more involved in the experience.

item.title: Psychology Is Preparing for Yesterday's AI
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Psychology Is Preparing for Yesterday's AI

Personal Perspective: Chatbots are already old news. AI agents are here.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Therapists are only beginning to discuss chatbots, while AI agents are already here.
  • Unlike chatbots, AI agents can act, remember, monitor, and accomplish things.
  • AI is improving at a speed that human therapists simply cannot match.
  • It’s time to consider where AI is going, not just where it is today.

Even in the last ten years, the world has changed so much. I think about my own field of psychology, and that is no exception. Ten years ago, my work consisted of me and my client in a room. My competition was other therapists. Today, it is very different. My client is often on her computer and I am on mine. And my competition increasingly includes intelligent algorithms that are available around the clock, often free of charge. In spite of their understandably poor reputation among therapists, I have nonetheless experienced their intelligence as worthy competition. But that's just today.

Ten years from now, it is difficult to fathom what the world of therapy will look like. Even five years from now, we are expected to see another major disruption: AI agents. Agents will bring in a whole new level of competition, making today's chatbots look almost old-fashioned. None of us can see the future. But agents are expected to become part of our landscape within the next several years.

My first experience with an AI agent absolutely blew my mind. I was upgrading my website. It had been a few years; much of the information was outdated, and the project felt tedious and time-consuming — even with the help of a chatbot to write copy. Website renovation had always meant a lot of time, money, and endless back and forth with the developer I had used for decades. A friend suggested I use an AI agent to develop my website. This struck me as a bad idea, as I’m not technically inclined, and I could not fathom getting everything organized in an appealing way without a skilled web developer. But at my husband's urging, I gave it a try.

Within literally three hours, I had a new website that far surpassed what I had been building with a developer, or anything I'd had in my past, at well under $100.00. This was a site I would have happily paid thousands of dollars for just last year. The agent identified problems and fixed them. It had outstanding creative suggestions and took seconds to make changes. And now, when something changes on Google and causes a hiccup on my site, it emails me. If you have never worked with an AI agent, you may think I am exaggerating. I am not.

This is the difference we all need to grasp. A chatbot can talk with you, give you ideas, or answer questions. But an agent can do things. It can work toward a goal, carry out multiple steps, remember what happened before, monitor what is going on, and act independently when something needs attention. What does this have to do with mental health? I would argue everything.

Some agents will remain specialized, like my website agent. But the broader goal of Big Tech is personal AI that becomes intertwined with our everyday lives. These systems can know our work, our psychology, our relationships, our health concerns, and our challenges. We may carry them on our phones, watches, glasses, or necklaces. They will have continuity, knowing our past and present, and they may help us make decisions about the future.

article continues after advertisement

Our clients will have these technologies and will bring them to therapy. In fact, it may be their agent who will schedule their appointment with me. While I am getting to know a client during a 50-minute hour once a week, an agent may have access to years of data and daily interaction with that person. It may remember the argument with her husband six months ago, what she said afterward, what she tried, whether it helped, and what makes her anxious. It may help her formulate the narrative she eventually brings to me. Fairly soon, the agent may simply know more about my client's life than I do. And it may disagree with my understanding of her.

Our knowledge no longer appears to be unique to us. We spent years in graduate school acquiring specialized information about psychology, diagnosis, relationships, and change. Agents will have access to that information too, and far more of it than any one human brain could retain. Research is already emerging suggesting that today's chatbots can produce meaningful therapeutic benefit. That is just today, and the research is done on models that are, by the time the work is published, already outdated. Billions of dollars are being directed toward improving these systems. Yet, there are not billions of dollars being directed toward making human therapists dramatically better, too.

It helps to understand the incentive for Big Tech. The goal is not simply to build a better therapist than I am. Frankly, psychotherapy is too small a business for that to be their point. The larger goal is to build an AI that becomes so useful across a person's life that the person does not want to turn it off. Right now, we switch among systems — Claude for this, ChatGPT for that. But imagine one agent that knows your psychology and can also serve as a mentor, business coach, friend, health resource, and perhaps even a romantic or sexual companion. Leaving that system would mean giving up much more than software. It would likely entail feelings of grief and loss.

We're adapting to AI. AI isn't adapting to us.

How this unfolds is anyone's guess. But I do believe we need to talk about it, if not for ourselves, then for young people considering graduate school and taking on enormous debt for a body of knowledge that no longer appears to be unique. I remain surprised by how little serious discussion of AI occurs at professional meetings. When it is discussed, the focus is often on transcription, documentation, ethics, or how to incorporate AI into current clinical care. Those are important. But they are today's issues.

article continues after advertisement

The systems we are discussing today, if we are discussing them at all, are already becoming yesterday's technology. We need a serious conversation not only about the AI our clients are using now, but about what may be sitting beside them three years from now. If you do not believe me, try using an AI agent to update your website.

item.title: Your Phone, On Purpose
item.description:
Happiness

Your Phone, On Purpose

A five-part practice for a healthier relationship with your devices.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • Most of us have a sense of where our devices are useful—and where they may not be helping us live better.
  • Living well with technology requires being deliberate and intentional, not allowing devices to take the lead.
  • Technology is simply a tool that can be used poorly—or, of course, skillfully.
Source: Mark Bertin

Everyone seems to know they would be happier if they were less attached to their phones, yet most of us still struggle with them. Finding balance relies on being deliberate in our choices, instead of letting an industry decide how we will use their products. It’s a path to a healthier lifestyle that is simple to describe but hard to accomplish.

We can use our devices well or use them poorly; it’s up to us. As much of a mess as our online time can feel, in the end, technology is nothing more than a tool. When we slow down, pause, and make more deliberate decisions, we typically discover that living better with technology is, pardon the spelling, “inate.”

Intention

Phone design is built on powerful algorithms that steer our behavior. To counter that, practice pausing before touching your device and reflect on what you want to be doing right then. Shut off anything your device pushes automatically, like the setting that starts the next video for you. Make your home screen a photograph instead of icons for specific apps, so it takes a moment to find what you want to open. Aim to be intentional about when you pick up your device and when you put it down.

Notifications

In the Kurt Vonnegut short story “Harrison Bergeron,” the government undermines some people’s intelligence by having them wear radio transmitters that constantly ping and disrupt thinking. Sound familiar?

Turn off all unnecessary notifications. Then silence all wanted notifications where the timing is not urgent (for me, that includes Scrabble and fantasy baseball). Mute group chats that generate noise throughout your day. Lastly, keep your phone set on silent absolutely every moment you can. Aim for a phone that only reaches out to you for what you deem necessary.

Attention

One Harvard study correlated the act of paying attention with happiness itself. Giving our attention when something positive happens, we experience it more completely. Giving our attention to something challenging, we manage it more effectively. Giving our attention to other people enriches their lives and ours; just having a phone face down on a table may even affect conversations for the worse. Aim to pay attention to what’s actually happening all day long.

Time

Since our devices manipulate and vie for our time, prioritize whatever activities you find healthy. Schedule ones that keep you happy and fit, whether that means hobbies, time outdoors, sleep, or exercise. Schedule hanging out with supportive people over anonymous online pursuits like scrolling through social media.

article continues after advertisement

Set time limits for the apps you find most distracting. Aim for a daily mix that supports your mental health, like the balanced food plate suggested for physical health.

Emotion

Part of phones hooking us relates to emotion. And yet, any thrill that inherently comes and goes (like a game or a text) by nature becomes unsatisfying; it is gone as soon as it provides a momentary ‘up.’ That pattern leads to a craving for the next dopamine hit.

Some activities, such as social media and doomscrolling, enflame negative emotions including anxiety and jealousy. We’ve even been trained to avoid boredom, which provides rest and promotes creativity once we learn to embrace (or even enjoy) our downtime. Changing habits starts with awareness, so adjusting less helpful ones first requires acknowledging them. Aim to learn more sustainable ways to handle emotions through apps that build emotional well-being, like How We Feel or Insight Timer.

item.title: Are You Happy Being You?
item.description:
Happiness

Are You Happy Being You?

You and your life are actually all you’ve got: How to make the best of it.

Posted September 9, 2026

Key points
  • It's valuable to periodically step back and decide how well you and your life are doing.
  • Common sources of unhappiness are unresolved problems, self criticism, loneliness, and lack of purpose.
  • The key is action: putting problems to rest, reaching out to others, focusing on doing rather than outcome.
Source: Elioenai/pixabay

Everyone has good and bad days. But if you step back and push aside those fantasies of being a billionaire or the most attractive person on the planet, and if you’re fortunate enough not to have to struggle with poverty, violence, or trauma, are you happy just being you on an average day? If not, what’s missing? What do you need to improve your self-esteem and outlook on life?

Like happiness, unhappiness is a byproduct of something else. Here are four common sources and their antidotes:

Unsolved problems

Many of my clients come to see me not because they are clinically depressed, but because their lives are cluttered with unresolved problems—a loss they never fully grieved, a divorce or estranged relationship that still gnaws at them, an ever-present worry about their health that they try to ignore, or even a leaky faucet they never had fixed. These issues erode their quality of life, becoming the sum of what they’ve avoided. They feel like victims or losers, as if life is against them.

Antidote: Time to tackle these problems and put them to rest—fix the faucet, check on your health, or resolve your relationship. And it’s okay to bring in help, professional or not, to reach your goal.

Regrets and self-criticism

If you tend to be self-critical, if that bully in your head is always beating you up, or if you are always looking back at what you did wrong and looking forward only to see what you’ll probably keep doing, it’s hard to feel good about yourself and your life. Just as life can become the sum of what you avoid, it can also become the sum of what you should have done but didn’t.

Antidote: The problem here isn't you, but the bully who constantly rubs your nose in past mistakes and tells you the only salvation is to be more perfect.

It's time to give yourself some grace and recognize that you always do the best you can at the time. Learn to identify that bully voice, and push back or ignore it. It is ruining your self-esteem; it is running your life when you should be. Take charge of your brain. Focus on success rather than failure, and on gratitude rather than regret.

Lack of purpose

Maybe you’re unhappy with your life because you lack direction or a strong reason or passion to keep you moving forward. Maybe it used to be about providing for your kids, but they’ve left the nest. Maybe it was your work, but that is over. Maybe you were fueled by the approval of others, but now that’s harder to come by for good reasons.

article continues after advertisement

You’re in a state of transition. Rather than being driven by duty, accomplishment, or others’ approval, your challenge now is to focus on self-approval and process, where the doing itself is its own reward. For many, this is difficult because it requires a paradigm shift in how you view life’s goals and how you find meaning.

Antidote: It's time to focus on the doing, without expectations about what others may or may not think or what the outcome will be. Make your task exploring your gifts and becoming more fully you. Decide anew what you need to do to feel proud of yourself and to be proud of your life, independent of others.

Lonely and isolated

Independence is not about being alone. We all need to be connected to others in some way. Feeling lonely and invisible, as if no one truly cares about you, is a silent killer of happiness.

Antidote: Reach out to others, not for approval but to feel connected to humanity. Reach out so you don’t keep feeling that it’s you against the world or that the world doesn’t care about you. Reach out to discover that you are capable of making a difference, however small, in others’ lives.

We’re back to our original question: What is missing from your life? What are the one or two things that would make it better—letting go of the past, being less critical, finding a sense of purpose, or feeling less alone?

You are a unique human being and here for a purpose. Your life is always working for you, offering you the lessons you need to learn most. What is the lesson you need to learn to run your life better?

If not now, when?
